newsitem.title: Bulgaria: Bulgaria Socialists cling to power despite clashes.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria Socialists cling to power despite clashes.

text.p: Bulgarian opposition protesters clashed with police on Saturday after security forces broke up a 10-hour siege of parliament but the ex-communist ruling party appeared determined to cling to power.

Crisis talks between President Zhelyu Zhelev and political and security chiefs, including opposition leaders, ended without agreement and Yordan Sokolov, parliamentary leader of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), said they might no longer be able to control protests.
Zhelev, meanwhile, was quoted as saying early elections were the only solution.
The UDF appealed for calm. "Don't be drawn into a gigantic communist provocation," said a message broadcast every half hour by private Darik radio.
"Belgrade has withstood for 50 days without being drawn into provocation," it said, referring to protests against the Socialist government in neighbouring Yugoslavia.

Scuffles broke out outside the presidency as Zhelev's meeting began. Protesters taunted police outside parliament, where riot police used clubs to break up a 10-hour opposition siege early on Saturday in the worst violence since the collapse of one-party communist rule in 1989.
As the protests entered their sixth consecutive day, Zhelev said he would not ask the Socialists to form a new government on Saturday as expected.
But state news agency BTA quoted Krassimir Premyanov, head of the Socialists' parliamentary group, as saying the party would not give up its mandate.
The Promyana (Change) trade union said miners in the Rhodope mountains and port workers in Varna would go on strike from Monday, and Sofia taxi drivers planned a protest parade.
Sofia university students declared a strike and unlikely support came from Bulgaria's tiny rump Communist Party, which issued a declaration saying it supported the protests.
Most former Communist leaders hastily re-formed as the Bulgarian Socialist Party in 1990.
"For the first time we are proud that we are Bulgarians, that the whole world is watching us. We hope that we will do even better than our brothers the Serbs," said Dimitar Trifonov, 33.
Russia voiced its concern over growing tensions in Bulgaria, which it described as a friendly state once seen as an "island of stability" in the troubled Balkans.
A statement issued by the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow hoped the crisis would be resolved "through dialogue within the constitution and democratic traditions".
Protests took place in half a dozen Bulgarian cities on Friday. BTA said local authorities in the Lovec region, which groups four large provincial towns, had banned mass gatherings.
In Paris, Le Monde newspaper quoted President Zhelev as saying an early general election was needed.
"Our country needs far more wide-ranging reforms than those proposed by the current political forces," he said in an interview with the paper published on Saturday.
"One can only hope to get out of this very serious situation...by organising early elections."

The confrontation, spurred by acute economic crisis, came after the governing Socialist Party refused to vote on Friday on a motion calling for fresh elections. The UDF walked out and urged a nationwide strike and civil disobedience.

What began with a human chain around the parliament building on Friday turned into a siege, trapping Socialist deputies. The demonstrators broke windows in parliament and smashed and overturned deputies' cars parked outside.
In the early hours of Saturday police moved in, using clubs and firing blank cartridges to beat a path into parliament to allow the Socialist deputies out.

At least 104 people were treated in hospital, among them three UDF deputies, four security guards from parliament and eight police. Former UDF prime minister Filip Dimitrov needed surgery for a head injury.
